quarterly_data.signal: Q4 and full-year 2025 results (quarter and year ended December 31, 2025), per CFO: Q4 product revenue $92.7 million, up 4.5% from Q3's $88.7 million and up 15.3% year over year; Q4 royalty revenue $14.5 million, a 33.1% sequential decrease because Q3 included a catch-up amount; Advanced Products share of total revenue (incl. royalties) 58.4% vs 59.4% in Q3; consolidated gross margin 55.4%; operating income $15.7 million (14.6% operating margin); Q4 tax benefit of approximately $27.3 million from partial recognition of deferred tax assets. FY2025: product revenue $350.3 million (+12.1%); royalty revenue $57.4 million (+23.2%, excludes the patent litigation settlement); total product + royalty revenue including a $45 million patent litigation settlement $452.7 million (+26.1%); Brick Products $159.1 million (-1.6%); gross margin 57.3% (from 51.2%); operating income $81.8 million; net income $118.6 million; diluted EPS $2.61 (from $0.14). Cash and cash equivalents $402.8 million. No quarterly guidance is given because the timing and amounts of licensing outcomes cannot be predicted.
quarterly_data.figure: Q4 product revenue $92.7 million (+4.5% QoQ, +15.3% YoY); royalty $14.5 million; GM 55.4%; FY2025 revenue $452.7 million (+26.1%, incl. $45 million settlement); FY GM 57.3%

quarterly_data.signal: Bookings inflecting: Q4 book-to-bill improved sequentially to 'over 1.2' and 'has continued to increase in Q1' (mid-Q1 update from the VP of Sales: 'we're above that already in Q1'); one-year backlog rose 15.8% from the prior quarter at year-end. Management says 2026 'should result in record bookings, revenues and profitability and significantly higher utilization of our first chip fab'; the CEO sees 2026 as 'one of major increase in product revenue, well above the rate of last year', which is 'pretty much baked in at this point based on bookings that we received' plus bookings expected during the year. Demand is increasing on a number of fronts: high-end computing plus automatic test equipment (ATE). The industrial and aerospace & defense outlook for 2026 is strong, with the ATE market 'projecting high growth to last for the next several years'; the VP of Sales is confident Vicor can 'double the revenues in these markets over the next 4 to 6 years'. Brick products are expected to stay fairly stable.
quarterly_data.figure: Q4 book-to-bill over 1.2 (higher so far in Q1); 1-year backlog +15.8% QoQ

quarterly_data.signal: Fab 1 (Andover) capacity: the CEO says that, given dollars per panel and panel throughput, Fab 1 can generate 'slightly above $1 billion' of revenue a year (confirmed for Advanced Products), with about 80% utilization as the practical target. Based on customer ramps 'with a strong contribution from high-end computing', he sees 'the existing fab being well utilized within a year', and he agreed with an analyst's reading that demand will reach a run rate using '80% or so of the capacity' (he confirmed the analyst's implied $800 million product-revenue level as 'a run rate', not as 2026 revenue). Fab 1 capacity is 'getting earmarked for strategic customers'; Vicor is adding capacity incrementally within the existing footprint and has begun engaging customers in capacity reservation agreements. Revenue from those agreements is recognized as products ship: a cash component shows up on the balance sheet, with no revenue acceleration.
quarterly_data.figure: Fab 1 capacity slightly above $1 billion a year; ~80% utilization run rate expected within a year

quarterly_data.signal: Capacity expansion: a second chip fab is in planning. Vicor has made 2 offers on land for a campus that could support up to 0.5 million square feet of manufacturing space (the current facility is around 300,000), with a 1.5 to 2 year lead time. It is also looking at existing buildings within a 30-mile radius north and west of Andover, which would cut the time to completion. No decision has been made, but the CEO expects Vicor is 'likely to do something on this soon'. He sizes the second facility at 'of the order of $250 million, $300 million', self-financed from Vicor's cash and balance sheet, at the same scale of capacity increment; additional capacity from the second fab 'may not be available until 2028'. Vicor is also in discussions with candidates for an alternate source of high-current-density Gen 5 VPD, which customers want and which would use the partner's own capabilities with Vicor technology; the CEO says 'there is no way that Vicor alone could do it even with the second and third fab'. Q4 capex was $5.5 million; construction in progress, mainly manufacturing equipment, was approximately $7.8 million, with approximately $6.9 million still to be spent.
quarterly_data.figure: 2nd fab cost of the order of $250 million, $300 million; new capacity may not be available until 2028; Q4 capex $5.5 million

quarterly_data.signal: IP licensing: the US International Trade Commission has instituted a second investigation into illegal importation of power modules and computing systems that infringe Vicor IP related to non-isolated bus converters. Management warns that unlicensed OEMs and hyperscalers face potential exclusion orders and urges them to take a license. Vicor has 2 major licensees in high-end computing AI and expects 'a lot more'. Asked how many major licensees it would have if things went well, the CEO said about 'half a dozen' substantial licensees in that market ('3x as many as we currently have') plus minor ones. The CEO expects 'hundreds of millions of dollars worth of revenues from licensing' and 'more patent settlements'. An analyst raised the roughly $300 million revenue goal from royalties plus licensee business, and the CEO repeated it as 'a relatively near-term goal, not for this year', within 'a couple of years' time frame'. The CFO noted that 2025 royalty revenue of $57.4 million excludes the patent litigation settlement.
quarterly_data.figure: 2 major licensees in high-end computing AI; about half a dozen substantial licensees if things go well

quarterly_data.signal: VPD lead customer (not named on this call) is ramping a Gen 4 factorized power system before transitioning to a Gen 5-based solution with higher current density and performance. The transition is expected to start in the second half of 2026, while Gen 4 production continues to 'ramp at a steep rate to the end of 2026'. According to the CEO, the Gen 4 system is mature, but the customer's next-generation system as a whole 'isn't quite there yet'. By year-end the lead customer will be using 'a significant share of our capacity' on the earlier generation, and the next-generation system adds 'an additional layer of use of capacity' into next year. Other Gen 5 (second-gen) VPD engagements will be selective: over the next couple of weeks, the global FAE team is being trained on Gen 5 VPD demo boards before engaging target hyperscalers and OEM chip companies. One prospect 'alone fill 2 fabs', and an automotive customer has shown interest. The VP of Sales says one very, very large company uses vertical power delivery in very high volume today (increasing year on year); high-volume use by anyone else is 'fairly limited', with others 'all trying to get Gen 1 VPD to work' and none he knows of deploying it in volume yet. The CEO says second-gen VPD with fifth-generation modules has much higher density, needs no stacking and is more efficient.
quarterly_data.figure: lead customer Gen 4 -> Gen 5 VPD transition to start in second half of 2026; Gen 4 ramping steeply to end of 2026

quarterly_data.signal: Content per accelerator: the VP of Sales puts Vicor's second-gen VPD opportunity at 'somewhere between $200 to $400 per XPU', depending on the XPU's current and number of rails. The CEO added 'Take that with a grain of salt' and clarified it is 'about like a 2,000 amp up to a 4,000 amp type of product'. For context, the CEO said a GPU power-system opportunity a number of years ago was 'about $100 million per year'. 'We are locking into an opportunity that will double that', he said, and a hyperscaler opportunity 'could be another'.
quarterly_data.figure: $200 to $400 per XPU; 2,000 amp up to a 4,000 amp product

quarterly_data.signal: 800-volt datacenter power: Vicor 'pioneered high-density' conversion from 800 volt and 400 volts and holds relevant IP and products, with 'more products in the pipeline that will come out later this year'. The CEO calls much of the 800-volt focus 'hype' and 'a diversion'. In his view an 800-volt bus is worth 'a few percent' in efficiency, while an inferior point-of-load solution loses '15 or 20 points'. GPU performance is gated by the point-of-load power system, where multiphase mainstream solutions are 'handicap', not by the choice of 48 volt or 800 volt distribution.
quarterly_data.figure: 800-volt bus: a few percent efficiency vs 15 or 20 points lost at point of load
